claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (D'Amour et al., 2006).

claims.claim: A low level of endogenous WNT activity is detectable in undifferentiated hPS cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, a low level of endogenous WNT activity is detectable in undifferentiated hPS cells (Blauwkamp et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2013) and is required for reprogramming of human fibroblasts to an induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell state (Ross et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Blauwkamp et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Endogenous WNT activity is required for reprogramming of human fibroblasts to an induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell state.
claims.source: Furthermore, a low level of endogenous WNT activity is detectable in undifferentiated hPS cells (Blauwkamp et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2013) and is required for reprogramming of human fibroblasts to an induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell state (Ross et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (Ross et al., 2014).

claims.claim: FZD7 plays a prominent role in the regulation of pluripotency of hPS cells.
claims.source: The WNT receptor FZD7 plays a prominent role in the regulation of pluripotency of hPS cells (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008), and its downregulation accompanies differentiation and exit from the pluripotent stem cell state.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).

claims.claim: Downregulation of FZD7 accompanies differentiation and exit from the pluripotent stem cell state.
claims.source: The WNT receptor FZD7 plays a prominent role in the regulation of pluripotency of hPS cells (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008), and its downregulation accompanies differentiation and exit from the pluripotent stem cell state.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).

claims.claim: hPS cells express several WNT receptors, including FZD2, 3, and 5.
claims.source: However, since hPS cells express several WNT receptors, including FZD2, 3, and 5 (Fernandez et al., 2014; Huggins et al., 2017), it is unclear whether Wnt3a promotes mesendodermal differentiation through FZD7 or whether other FZDs are required.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Fernandez et al., 2014; Huggins et al., 2017).

claims.claim: F7-Ab is a chimeric human/mouse IgG1 antibody derived from a bacterially produced antigen binding fragment (Fab).
claims.source: We generated a single-chain variable fragment (scFv) to FZD7 by repurposing the variable region of our FZD7-targeting antibody (F7-Ab), a chimeric human/mouse IgG1. This antibody was derived from a bacterially produced antigen binding fragment (Fab) described in a previous study (Fernandez et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study (Fernandez et al., 2014) and describes the experimental design.

claims.claim: F7L6 was engineered by conjugating the FZD7-scFv and LRP6-scFv to a human IgG1 Fc.
claims.source: We then engineered F7L6 by conjugating the FZD7-scFv and LRP6-scFv to a human IgG1 Fc to create the FZD7-specific Wnt mimetic F7L6 (complete amino acid sequence is provided in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design and construction of F7L6, with reference to a figure showing the sequence.

claims.claim: F7-Ab, F7, L6, and F7L6 are secreted from CHO cells.
claims.source: We confirmed secretion of F7-Ab, F7, L6, and F7L6 from CHO cells by SDS-PAGE and Coomassie Blue staining and immunoblotting (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: FZD7-specific binders (F7 and F7L6) only react with lysates upon FZD7 overexpression.
claims.source: FZD7-specific binders (F7 and F7L6) only reacted with lysates upon FZD7 overexpression (note that endogenous FZD7 expression in LRP6 KO is below the level of detection), whereas LRP6-specific binders (L6 and F7L6) only reacted with lysates of cells expressing LRP6 (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C using dot blot assays.

claims.claim: LRP6-specific binders (L6 and F7L6) only react with lysates of cells expressing LRP6.
claims.source: FZD7-specific binders (F7 and F7L6) only reacted with lysates upon FZD7 overexpression (note that endogenous FZD7 expression in LRP6 KO is below the level of detection), whereas LRP6-specific binders (L6 and F7L6) only reacted with lysates of cells expressing LRP6 (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C using dot blot assays.

claims.claim: F7-Ab binds to the 'neck' region between the cysteine-rich domain (CRD) and the first transmembrane domain of FZD7.
claims.source: To further characterize the specificity of F7-Ab, we mapped its binding site to the 'neck' region between the cysteine-rich domain (CRD) and the first transmembrane domain of FZD7 (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from epitope mapping experiments shown in Figure 1D-F.

claims.claim: F7-Ab only reacts with human FZD7 (hFZD7) and not with mouse Fzd7 (mFzd7).
claims.source: Despite the high degree of homology between human and mouse Fzd7 (hFZD7 and mFzd7, respectively), F7-Ab only reacts with hFZD7 (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: A single amino acid change at position 188 from leucine to proline (P188) renders hFZD7 non-reactive to F7-Ab.
claims.source: A single amino acid change at position 188 from leucine to proline (P188) renders hFZD7 non-reactive to F7-Ab, whereas the corresponding amino acid change in mFzd7 (L188) restores F7-Ab reactivity (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E using mutant constructs.

claims.claim: The F7-Ab epitope maps to an eight amino acid stretch containing L188.
claims.source: Using fusion proteins between glutathione S-transferase (GST) and the FZD7 neck region followed by sequential shortening of the neck region, we mapped the F7-Ab epitope to an eight amino acid stretch containing L188 (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F using GST fusion proteins.

claims.claim: F7-Ab does not cross-react with the other nine human FZD receptors (FZD1-6, 8–10).
claims.source: Since FZD proteins are highly conserved and several available FZD antibodies react with multiple FZD proteins (for example, OMP-18R5/Vantictumab reacts with FZD1, 2, 5, 7, and 8), we confirmed that F7-Ab does not cross-react with the other nine human FZD receptors (FZD1-6, 8–10) (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G using flow cytometry.

claims.claim: All FZD proteins (FZD1-10) are expressed on the cell surface.
claims.source: To rule out the possibility that some FZDs fail to react with F7-Ab because they do not reach the cell surface, we performed confocal microscopy. This analysis confirmed that all FZD proteins were expressed on the cell surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 using confocal microscopy.

claims.claim: F7-Ab, F7, and F7L6 are specific to hFZD7 and do not cross-react with any of the other nine human FZD proteins or with mFzd7.
claims.source: Taken together, F7-Ab, and hence F7 and F7L6, are specific to hFZD7 and do not cross-react with any of the other nine human FZD proteins or with mFzd7.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: F7L6 activates WNT/β-catenin signaling by heterodimerizing FZD7 and LRP6.
claims.source: The bispecific binder, F7L6, activates WNT/β-catenin signaling by heterodimerizing FZD7 and LRP6 (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: F7L6 activates the Super TOP-Flash (STF) WNT reporter in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: We confirmed F7L6 signaling activity using HEK293T cells stably transfected with the WNT reporter Super TOP-Flash (STF) (Veeman et al., 2003; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B using luciferase reporter assays.

claims.claim: Single binders to FZD7 (F7) or LRP6 (L6) do not activate WNT signaling.
claims.source: As expected, single binders to FZD7 (F7) or LRP6 (L6) did not activate signaling.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Activity of F7L6 is potently augmented by addition of R-Spondin1 (RSPO1).
claims.source: As is the case with native WNT proteins, activity of F7L6 is potently augmented by addition of R-Spondin1 (RSPO1) (Kim et al., 2008; Figure 2C) with potency in the single-digit nanomolar range.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and a citation to prior work (Kim et al., 2008).

claims.claim: Addition of RSPO1 increased F7L6 activity approximately 10-fold.
claims.source: Interestingly, addition of RSPO1 increased F7L6 activity approximately 10-fold, but only augmented the activities of Wnt3a or FLAg FP+P-L1+3, a previously published WNT mimetic (Tao et al., 2019), by twofold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Addition of RSPO1 augmented the activities of Wnt3a or FLAg FP+P-L1+3 by twofold.
claims.source: Interestingly, addition of RSPO1 increased F7L6 activity approximately 10-fold, but only augmented the activities of Wnt3a or FLAg FP+P-L1+3, a previously published WNT mimetic (Tao et al., 2019), by twofold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: F7L6 is selective for FZD7, whereas Wnt3a and FLAg FP+P-L1+3 are capable of interacting with multiple FZDs.
claims.source: A possible reason for this distinction is that F7L6 is selective for FZD7, whereas Wnt3a and FLAg FP+P-L1+3 are capable of interacting with multiple FZDs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in RSPO1 augmentation and known properties of the molecules.

claims.claim: F7L6 and FLAg FP+P-L1+3 retain significant activity at sub-nanomolar concentrations, whereas Wnt3a's activity is undetectable at such concentrations.
claims.source: Furthermore, both Wnt mimetics retain significant activity at sub-nanomolar concentrations, whereas Wnt3a's activity is undetectable at such concentrations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dose-response curves shown in the figures.

claims.claim: F7L6 activates signaling independently of the WNT-binding cysteine-rich domain (CRD) of FZD7.
claims.source: Interestingly, FZD7 lacking the CRD (CRD-less FZD7) activates signaling when heterodimerized to LRP6 with F7L6 while Wnt3a does not (Figure 2D), indicating that the CRD is dispensable for signaling.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D using CRD-deleted FZD7 constructs.

claims.claim: The CRD of FZD7 is dispensable for WNT signaling when FZD7 is heterodimerized with LRP6 by F7L6.
claims.source: Interestingly, FZD7 lacking the CRD (CRD-less FZD7) activates signaling when heterodimerized to LRP6 with F7L6 while Wnt3a does not (Figure 2D), indicating that the CRD is dispensable for signaling.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and represents an inference from the data.

claims.claim: Appending the F7-Ab epitope of eight amino acids onto FZD2 is sufficient for F7L6 to activate WNT/β-catenin signaling through FZD2.
claims.source: Furthermore, appending the F7-Ab epitope of eight amino acids (see Figure 1F) onto another FZD, FZD2, is sufficient for F7L6 to activate WNT/β-catenin signaling through FZD2 (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E using FZD2 with the appended epitope.

claims.claim: Heterodimerization of FZD7 or FZD2 with LRP6 is sufficient for WNT pathway activation.
claims.source: These data establish that heterodimerization of FZD7 or FZD2 with LRP6 is sufficient for pathway activation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from Figures 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: Treatment of mouse L-cells with Wnt3a activates downstream signaling, as assayed by cytoplasmic β-catenin stabilization.
claims.source: Treatment of mouse L-cells with Wnt3a activates downstream signaling, as assayed by cytoplasmic β-catenin stabilization (Shibamoto et al., 1998), whereas treatment with F7L6 does not (Figure 2F), consistent with the lack of reactivity of F7-Ab with mouse Fzd7 (see Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and a citation to prior work (Shibamoto et al., 1998).

claims.claim: Treatment of mouse L-cells with F7L6 does not activate downstream signaling.
claims.source: Treatment of mouse L-cells with Wnt3a activates downstream signaling, as assayed by cytoplasmic β-catenin stabilization (Shibamoto et al., 1998), whereas treatment with F7L6 does not (Figure 2F), consistent with the lack of reactivity of F7-Ab with mouse Fzd7 (see Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Overexpression of human FZD7 in mouse L-cells is sufficient to activate signaling by F7L6.
claims.source: However, overexpression of human FZD7 in these cells is sufficient to activate signaling by F7L6 (Figure 2F), thus confirming F7L6 signaling specificity through FZD7.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The kinetics of β-catenin stabilization in L-cells is similar for Wnt3a and F7L6, being first detectable between 15 and 30 min after stimulation.
claims.source: The kinetics of β-catenin stabilization in L-cells is similar for Wnt3a and F7L6, being first detectable between 15 and 30 min after stimulation (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G using time-course immunoblotting.

claims.claim: F7L6 activates expression of the WNT target gene SP5 in hPS cells in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: Lastly, using reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), we demonstrated that F7L6, like Wnt3a, activates expression of the WNT target gene, SP5, in hPS cells, which express FZD7 (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008), in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: F7L6 is a bispecific bivalent (or tetravalent) molecule, potentially capable of simultaneously engaging two FZD7 and two LRP6 molecules.
claims.source: F7L6 is a bispecific bivalent (or tetravalent) molecule, potentially capable of simultaneously engaging two FZD7 and two LRP6 molecules, thus leading to receptor oligomerization, which has been proposed to promote intracellular signalosome formation (DeBruine et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on the molecular design of F7L6 and a citation to prior work on receptor oligomerization (DeBruine et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Receptor oligomerization has been proposed to promote intracellular signalosome formation.
claims.source: F7L6 is a bispecific bivalent (or tetravalent) molecule, potentially capable of simultaneously engaging two FZD7 and two LRP6 molecules, thus leading to receptor oligomerization, which has been proposed to promote intracellular signalosome formation (DeBruine et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work (DeBruine et al., 2017).

claims.claim: F7L6-sc is a single-chain version of F7L6 that is predicted to engage one FZD7 and one LRP6 receptor.
claims.source: To address whether FZD7-LRP6 heterodimerization alone is sufficient for signaling, we deleted the Fc portion to generate a single-chain F7L6 (F7L6-sc) that is predicted to engage one FZD7 and one LRP6 receptor.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of F7L6-sc.

claims.claim: F7L6-sc activated Wnt signaling, albeit to a lesser extent than the tetravalent F7L6 protein.
claims.source: F7L6-sc activated Wnt signaling, albeit to a lesser extent than the tetravalent F7L6 protein (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: The maximal response in the STF assay for F7L6 was approximately twice that for F7L6-sc.
claims.source: Interestingly, the maximal response in the STF assay for F7L6 was approximately twice that for F7L6-sc.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: F7L6-sc is monomeric in solution and does not form larger oligomers.
claims.source: Size exclusion chromatography confirmed that F7L6-sc is monomeric in solution and does not form larger oligomers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 using size exclusion chromatography.

claims.claim: A 1:1 association of FZD7 and LRP6 is sufficient to activate downstream WNT signaling.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that a 1:1 association of FZD7 and LRP6 is sufficient to activate downstream signaling.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from F7L6-sc experiments.

claims.claim: Modulating WNT/β-catenin signaling is crucial for differentiation of hPS cells into mesendoderm and definitive endoderm (DE).
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that modulating WNT/β-catenin signaling is crucial for differentiation of hPS cells into mesendoderm and DE (D'Amour et al., 2006; Huggins et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2013; Martyn et al., 2018; Yoney et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Wnt3a and GSK3-inhibitors are frequently used interchangeably as WNT pathway activators in differentiation protocols.
claims.source: Wnt3a and GSK3-inhibitors (e.g. CHIR99021, CHIR98014, BIO, Li) (Klein and Melton, 1996; Ring et al., 2003; Sato et al., 2004; Stambolic et al., 1996) are frequently used interchangeably as WNT pathway activators in these differentiation protocols (Gertow et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2015; Loh et al., 2014; Naujok et al., 2014; Teo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: FZD7 transduces the Wnt3a signal.
claims.source: We hypothesized that FZD7 mediates this process, because it transduces the Wnt3a signal (Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; Voloshanenko et al., 2017) and regulates the pluripotent state (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; Voloshanenko et al., 2017).

claims.claim: FZD7 regulates the pluripotent state of hPS cells.
claims.source: We hypothesized that FZD7 mediates this process, because it transduces the Wnt3a signal (Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; Voloshanenko et al., 2017) and regulates the pluripotent state (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies (Fernandez et al., 2014; Melchior et al., 2008).

claims.claim: F7L6, Wnt3a, and CHIR98014 treatment significantly altered expression of 525, 708, and 1646 genes, respectively.
claims.source: F7L6, Wnt3, and CHIR treatment significantly altered expression of 525, 708, and 1646 genes, respectively (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4 and supplementary files.

claims.claim: A majority of genes (428 of 805 genes) in the F7L6 and Wnt3a lists overlapped.
claims.source: A majority of genes (428 of 805 genes) (Supplementary file 1E and F) in the F7L6 and Wnt3a lists overlapped, whereas expression changes of a large number of genes was unique to CHIR (1009 genes) (Supplementary file 1G), highlighting the substantial differences when the pathway is activated at the level of receptor rather than at the level of GSK3 inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in supplementary files.

claims.claim: Expression changes of a large number of genes (1009 genes) was unique to CHIR treatment.
claims.source: A majority of genes (428 of 805 genes) (Supplementary file 1E and F) in the F7L6 and Wnt3a lists overlapped, whereas expression changes of a large number of genes was unique to CHIR (1009 genes) (Supplementary file 1G), highlighting the substantial differences when the pathway is activated at the level of receptor rather than at the level of GSK3 inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in supplementary files.

claims.claim: Gene expression changes in response to Wnt3a and F7L6 were overall highly similar.
claims.source: Gene expression changes in response to Wnt3a and F7L6 were overall highly similar, with robust activation of classic markers of mesendoderm (i.e. GSC, MIXL1, SP5 and T) and DE (i.e. LEFTY1, EOMES, CER1, FOXA2, CXCR4, and SOX17) and downregulation of pluripotency markers, such as POU3F1, FZD7, and PODXL (TRA-1–81).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Wnt3a and F7L6 treatment led to robust activation of classic markers of mesendoderm (GSC, MIXL1, SP5 and T) and DE (LEFTY1, EOMES, CER1, FOXA2, CXCR4, and SOX17).
claims.source: Gene expression changes in response to Wnt3a and F7L6 were overall highly similar, with robust activation of classic markers of mesendoderm (i.e. GSC, MIXL1, SP5 and T) and DE (i.e. LEFTY1, EOMES, CER1, FOXA2, CXCR4, and SOX17) and downregulation of pluripotency markers, such as POU3F1, FZD7, and PODXL (TRA-1–81).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Wnt3a and F7L6 treatment led to downregulation of pluripotency markers, such as POU3F1, FZD7, and PODXL (TRA-1–81).
claims.source: Gene expression changes in response to Wnt3a and F7L6 were overall highly similar, with robust activation of classic markers of mesendoderm (i.e. GSC, MIXL1, SP5 and T) and DE (i.e. LEFTY1, EOMES, CER1, FOXA2, CXCR4, and SOX17) and downregulation of pluripotency markers, such as POU3F1, FZD7, and PODXL (TRA-1–81).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Induction of established WNT target genes (DKK1, AXIN2, WLS, WNT3, and NKD1) was more potent with Wnt3a than with F7L6.
claims.source: However, there were some notable differences between Wnt3a and F7L6 treatments. For example, induction of established WNT target genes, such as DKK1, AXIN2, WLS, WNT3, and NKD1, was more potent with Wnt3a than with F7L6.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Induction of genes such as T, SP5, GSC, and FOXA2 was slightly delayed for F7L6 relative to Wnt3a.
claims.source: Also, induction of genes, such as T, SP5, GSC, and FOXA2, was slightly delayed for F7L6 relative to Wnt3a.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Differences between F7L6 and Wnt3a are potentially due to F7L6 solely engaging FZD7 and LRP6, while Wnt3a promotes signaling through multiple FZD-LRP5/6 heterodimers.
claims.source: These differences are potentially due to F7L6 solely engaging FZD7 and LRP6 to promote downstream signaling, while Wnt3a, in contrast, promotes signaling through multiple FZD-LRP5/6 heterodimers.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in gene expression and known properties of F7L6 and Wnt3a.

claims.claim: CHIR treatment produced significantly different gene expression profiles compared to Wnt3a and F7L6, both in kinetics and amplitude.
claims.source: In contrast to Wnt3a and F7L6, CHIR treatment produced significantly different gene expression profiles, both in kinetics and amplitude (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: All three treatments (F7L6, Wnt3a, and CHIR) activated known WNT target genes (AXIN2, DKK1, LEF1, and SP5) and mesendodermal genes (T, MIXL1, GATA4, and EOMES).
claims.source: For example, while all three treatments activated known WNT target genes (e.g. AXIN2, DKK1, LEF1, and SP5) and mesendodermal genes (e.g. T, MIXL1, GATA4, and EOMES), CHIR did so more robustly than Wnt3a or F7L6.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: CHIR activated WNT target genes and mesendodermal genes more robustly than Wnt3a or F7L6.
claims.source: For example, while all three treatments activated known WNT target genes (e.g. AXIN2, DKK1, LEF1, and SP5) and mesendodermal genes (e.g. T, MIXL1, GATA4, and EOMES), CHIR did so more robustly than Wnt3a or F7L6.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Differences in gene activation by CHIR are likely attributable to the fact that CHIR acts downstream of the receptor complexes and hence is not restricted by receptor availability.
claims.source: Such differences are likely attributable to the fact that CHIR acts downstream of the receptor complexes and hence is not restricted by receptor availability.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of action of CHIR as a GSK3 inhibitor.

claims.claim: CHIR failed to activate expression of certain definitive endoderm markers, in particular FOXA2 and SOX17.
claims.source: Furthermore, while all three treatments activated expression of Wnt pathway and mesendodermal genes, CHIR failed to activate expression of certain genes, in particular the DE markers FOXA2 and SOX 17 (and to a lesser extent CER and GSC), an effect we validated using RT-qPCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and RT-qPCR validation shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Expression of CXCR4, which encodes a cell surface receptor commonly used to enrich DE populations, was activated by CHIR.
claims.source: Interestingly, expression of other DE markers, such as CXCR4, which encodes a cell surface receptor commonly used to enrich DE populations using flow cytometry (D'Amour et al., 2005; McGrath et al., 1999), was activated by CHIR (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B and citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Sustained activation of WNT/β-catenin signaling by GSK3 inhibition with CHIR produces significant differences compared to selective pathway activation with either Wnt3a or F7L6.
claims.source: These results indicate that sustained activation of WNT/β-catenin signaling by GSK3 inhibition with CHIR produces significant differences compared to selective pathway activation with either Wnt3a or F7L6.

results.result: F7L6 is an engineered bispecific protein that selectively binds human FZD7 and LRP6. The FZD7-binding component (F7-Ab) targets an 8-amino acid epitope in the neck region of FZD7 containing leucine at position 188, and shows no cross-reactivity with other human FZD receptors (FZD1-6, 8-10) or mouse Fzd7.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C21-C32 collectively demonstrate F7L6 specificity through multiple complementary approaches: epitope mapping (C26, C28, C29), species selectivity testing (C27), cross-reactivity screening against all 10 FZD receptors (C30), and confocal microscopy confirming cell surface expression (C31). The experimental evidence from dot blots, flow cytometry, GST fusion proteins, and immunoblotting provides strong convergent support for the claimed selectivity.

results.result: F7L6 activates WNT/β-catenin signaling through heterodimerization of FZD7 and LRP6. F7L6 activates the STF reporter with single-digit nanomolar potency when augmented by RSPO1, shows species-specific activity (human FZD7 but not mouse Fzd7), and demonstrates that the CRD of FZD7 is dispensable for signaling when receptors are heterodimerized by F7L6.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C49 provide comprehensive functional validation through multiple assays: STF luciferase reporter (C34), β-catenin stabilization kinetics (C48), dose-response curves (C36, C40), species-specificity controls (C45-C47), and CRD-deletion experiments (C41-C42). The convergent evidence from different cell types and assay formats strongly supports the mechanism of action.

results.result: A 1:1 heterodimerization of FZD7 and LRP6 is sufficient for WNT pathway activation. The bivalent F7L6-sc (engaging one FZD7 and one LRP6) activates signaling, though with approximately half the maximal response of tetravalent F7L6, suggesting that receptor oligomerization may control signal amplitude but is not strictly required.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 demonstrate sufficiency of 1:1 receptor engagement through comparison of tetravalent F7L6 versus bivalent F7L6-sc. Size exclusion chromatography confirms F7L6-sc is monomeric (C55), and STF assays show reduced but significant activity (C53-C54). The twofold difference in maximal response provides quantitative support for the role of oligomerization in signal amplitude.

results.result: F7L6 and Wnt3a elicit highly similar transcriptional responses in hPS cells, activating mesendodermal and definitive endoderm markers while downregulating pluripotency markers. In contrast, GSK3 inhibition with CHIR produces significantly different gene expression profiles, failing to activate key endodermal markers FOXA2 and SOX17 despite activating WNT target genes and mesendodermal markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C76 are supported by comprehensive RNA-seq analysis showing 428 of 805 genes overlap between F7L6 and Wnt3a treatments (C62), with similar activation of mesendodermal/DE markers (C64-C66) and validation by RT-qPCR (C74). The distinct CHIR response is well-documented with 1009 unique genes (C63) and failure to activate FOXA2/SOX17 (C74). Minor differences between F7L6 and Wnt3a (C67-C68) are appropriately attributed to receptor selectivity (C69).

results.result: F7L6 and Wnt3a activate early WNT target genes with similar kinetics in hPS cells, supporting that FZD7-LRP6 heterodimerization is sufficient to elicit transcriptional responses without requiring recruitment of additional receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 are supported by RT-qPCR validation of multiple early target genes (AXIN2, SOX9, ARL4A at 3hr; NKX1-2, NKD1, FGF18 at 6hr) showing similar kinetics between F7L6 and Wnt3a. However, the inference that additional receptors are not involved (C79) is based on similarity of responses rather than direct exclusion experiments. The conclusion is reasonable but could benefit from additional mechanistic validation.

results.result: F7L6 potently activates T-GFP and SOX17-eGFP reporters in hPS cells with temporal kinetics similar to Wnt3a (T-GFP at 24hr, SOX17-eGFP at 36hr), though with higher potency than Wnt3a. CHIR treatment shows distinct kinetics with early T-GFP expression that declines and no SOX17-eGFP induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C86 are supported by live cell imaging data showing temporal activation patterns. The higher potency of F7L6 versus Wnt3a (C83) is attributed to Wnt3a instability (C84), which is a reasonable inference but not directly tested. The distinct CHIR response (C85-C86) is consistent with RNA-seq data and strengthens the conclusion that receptor-level activation differs from GSK3 inhibition.

results.result: Activation of FZD7 alone is sufficient to promote definitive endoderm formation. F7L6 treatment during DE differentiation leads to downregulation of pluripotency marker OCT4 and upregulation of endodermal markers (SOX17, CXCR4, FOXA2) to similar extents as Wnt3a.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 are supported by RT-qPCR data from directed DE differentiation experiments. The conclusion of sufficiency (C87) is well-supported by the similar efficacy of F7L6 (FZD7-selective) and Wnt3a (multi-FZD) in activating DE markers. The experimental design appropriately uses an established DE differentiation protocol with Activin A, providing relevant biological context.

results.result: Selective FZD7 activation with F7L6 hinders hematopoietic differentiation from hPS cells. F7L6 treatment significantly reduced CD34+/CD45+ double-positive cells and failed to induce hematopoietic markers (MESP1, MIXL1, KDR), demonstrating lineage-specific effects of FZD7 signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 are supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced CD34+/CD45+ cells (C91-C92) and RT-qPCR showing failure to induce hematopoietic markers (C93). This contrasts with prior work showing WNT9A/FZD9 promotes hematopoietic differentiation (C90), supporting the conclusion of lineage-specific FZD requirements (C94). The experimental design appropriately uses an established hematopoietic differentiation protocol.

results.result: Selective engagement and heterodimerization of FZD7 and LRP6 with F7L6 is sufficient to drive mesendodermal differentiation programs in hPS cells, eliciting transcriptional responses associated with primitive streak formation and gastrulation that are nearly identical to those induced by Wnt3a.
results.evaluation: Claims C95, C100-C101 represent the main conclusion of the manuscript, synthesizing results from multiple experimental approaches. The conclusion is well-supported by convergent evidence from RNA-seq (showing similar transcriptional responses), reporter assays (showing similar temporal kinetics), and directed differentiation experiments (showing similar DE formation). The comprehensive dataset provides strong support for the sufficiency of FZD7 signaling.

results.result: GSK3 inhibition with CHIR elicits significantly different effects compared to receptor-level WNT activation with Wnt3a or F7L6, failing to induce endodermal markers FOXA2 and SOX17 and showing different β-catenin dynamics. This demonstrates that specific activation of WNT/FZD signaling is important to recapitulate developmental processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 are supported by RNA-seq data (C103), RT-qPCR validation, reporter assays, and citation to prior work on β-catenin dynamics (C104). The conclusion about importance of receptor-level activation (C105) is well-justified by the consistent differences observed across multiple assays. This finding has important implications for differentiation protocols that use GSK3 inhibitors interchangeably with WNT proteins.

results.result: WNT mimetics like F7L6 offer advantages over native WNT proteins: greater receptor selectivity, improved physicochemical properties (soluble, stable in standard buffers), retention of activity at lower concentrations, and simpler purification (single affinity step, ~2.5 mg/L yield versus 0.1 mg/L for Wnt3a requiring 3-4 chromatography steps).
results.evaluation: Claims C109, C113, C117-C119 are supported by experimental data comparing F7L6 and Wnt3a properties (dose-response curves showing sub-nanomolar activity for F7L6, purification yields) and citations to prior work on WNT purification challenges (C114-C115). The advantages are well-documented, though the speculation about overcoming co-receptor requirements (C113) is appropriately qualified as potential rather than demonstrated.

results.result: F7L6 binds the neck region of FZD7 rather than the CRD, enabling exclusive FZD7 engagement. This demonstrates that the CRD has no additional role beyond docking WNT proteins, as CRD-less FZD7 can signal when heterodimerized with LRP6 by F7L6.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C123 are supported by epitope mapping data (C26, C29) and functional experiments with CRD-deleted FZD7 (C41-C42). The conclusion that the CRD has no additional signaling role (C123) is well-supported by the ability of CRD-less FZD7 to signal with F7L6 but not Wnt3a. This represents an important mechanistic insight into FZD receptor function.

results.result: Higher-order receptor oligomerization is not strictly required for WNT signaling but may control signal amplitude. Bivalent F7L6-sc (1:1 FZD7:LRP6) activates signaling, while tetravalent F7L6 shows approximately twofold greater maximal response, possibly through promoting receptor clustering and signalosome formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C128 integrate structural studies from prior work (C124) with experimental data comparing F7L6 and F7L6-sc (C53-C54, C126). The conclusion that oligomerization is not strictly required is well-supported (C126), while the proposed mechanism for amplitude control (C127) is appropriately presented as inference. The speculation about receptor clustering (C128) is reasonable but would benefit from additional mechanistic studies.
